clue.text: Suggestion from middleman oddly ignored

indicators.note: 'oddly' counts positions rather than describing behaviour, and 'ignored' throws those positions away, leaving every second letter standing.

parts.note: take the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of this word, in the order they come

explanation.surface: A go-between offers a proposal and nobody pays the slightest attention to it.
explanation.walkthrough: A middleman is exactly the sort of person whose advice gets waved away, which is what keeps 'oddly ignored' reading as rudeness instead of as an instruction about letter positions.
explanation.definitionFit: An idea put to somebody is a suggestion — the everyday sense of a proposal offered for consideration rather than a thought kept to yourself.

clue.text: Destroy spirit

definitions.meaning: the verb you use of a rumour or a plan you have put a decisive end to
the drinks-cabinet sense: the distilled stuff, not gin or brandy but the Scottish one

explanation.surface: Crushing somebody's morale, breaking their spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two senses, nothing to take apart. 'Spirit' is the bottle rather than the soul, and the drink loses its capital because the clue has to start somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: To scotch a rumour or a plan is to destroy it, and Scotch is whisky — the setter drops the capital letter that the drink normally carries.

clue.text: Showman, one playing Paris and Rome

indicators.note: An actor playing a part comes on as somebody other than themselves, and letters told to play arrive in a shape that is not their own.

parts.note: one = I, the Roman numeral
nine more letters of raw material, the two city names taken together

explanation.surface: A performer touring two great European capitals with the same production.
explanation.walkthrough: Paris and Rome look like the tour dates a showman would boast about, and they are the letters instead — which is the whole disguise, since a clue about theatre is entitled to mention cities.
explanation.definitionFit: An impresario is the person who puts on operas and concerts and sells them to the public, so 'showman' names the trade.

clue.text: Supply of suet for juvenile wannabe?

indicators.note: Not the noun about deliveries: read it as the adverb of supple, meaning limberly, and something limber bends into whatever shape you like.

parts.note: six letters of raw material, the little word counted in

explanation.surface: A butcher hands over suet to a youngster with ambitions in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' opens the clue looking like a noun about provisions, and the question mark is the setter admitting the definition is a joke about ambition rather than a dictionary entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A foetus is not a juvenile yet — 'wannabe' is doing the work, since it is a would-be child, still waiting to be born into the rank named.

clue.text: Infiltrate a couple's enthralling exchange at last

indicators.note: A thrall was a captive, so to enthral is to hold somebody fast, and what enthrals here keeps another letter shut inside it.

parts.note: 'per' stands in for 'a': five pounds per head is five pounds a head

indicators.note: 'at last' points at the end of the word in front of it, so only that word's final letter is wanted.

parts.note: to couple is to mate — animals do it in every nature documentary
the final letter of 'exchange'

explanation.surface: A couple trade a spellbinding last word and somebody works their way into the middle of it.
explanation.walkthrough: PER for 'a' is the piece worth keeping — a wage per week is a wage a week — and 'enthralling' reads as praise for the exchange rather than as the order it is.
explanation.definitionFit: To permeate something is to spread right through every part of it, which is what an infiltrator does to an organisation — both verbs mean getting in everywhere.

clue.text: Revolutionary cut more unusual root vegetable

indicators.note: A revolution takes a thing full circle, so the letters are read back the other way rather than as printed.
The barber's sense: take something off the end, which for a word means losing its final letter.

parts.note: more unusual = odder
the R is trimmed off the end, leaving four letters to turn round

explanation.surface: A radical trims back a strange-looking root on the vegetable plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' is a turn, not a person, despite a surface full of politics. The vegetable is one Caribbean and West African cooks know well and British supermarkets label as taro.
explanation.definitionFit: An eddo is the starchy tuber of the taro plant, a staple in Caribbean and West African cooking, so 'root vegetable' names its category.

clue.text: Average doctor taking nothing on

indicators.note: The swallowing sense: what a doctor takes goes inside them, so the letter named next is swallowed by the word for doctor.

parts.note: a medic is a doctor
O is nothing, the zero written as a ring
RE = on the subject of, the way a memo heading uses it

explanation.surface: A doctor accepts nothing at all on top of what they are already owed.
explanation.walkthrough: RE for 'on' is the memo convention — 'Re: the meeting' means on the subject of the meeting — and it is the last two letters solvers usually find here.
explanation.definitionFit: Average here means no better than the middle of the pack, the faintly disappointing sense — which is the only sense mediocre has.

clue.text: Claim written language doesn't include the letter R

indicators.note: It reads as a flat statement about the language and works as an order: whatever is named after it has to come out.

parts.note: prose is written language, as opposed to verse
the setter names the letter outright, and this is the one that goes

explanation.surface: A pedant insisting that written language leaves the letter R out.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue asserts something plainly untrue about English, and that flat wrongness is the disguise — it is not a fact at all but an instruction to remove a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To pose as a doctor is to claim to be one, so 'claim' is the verb of pretence rather than of demanding what you are owed.

clue.text: Go off Geordie TV presenter, old male model

parts.note: Dec is Declan Donnelly, the shorter half of the Newcastle double act Ant and Dec — a Geordie is someone from Tyneside
O = old, standard abbreviation
M = male, standard abbreviation
to model for a painter or a photographer is to pose

explanation.surface: A viewer has gone off a Geordie presenter and an ageing male model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go off' is milk, not affection, which the celebrity surface works hard to hide. Ant and Dec have presented Saturday-night television together for thirty years, and setters use 'Geordie' to point at either name.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that goes off decomposes: 'go off' is the British idiom for rotting, and it matches as a verb phrase.

clue.text: Because of two performers, start to obfuscate

parts.note: two performers singing together make a duet

indicators.note: 'start' asks for the opening letter of the word that follows and nothing else of it.

parts.note: the first letter of 'obfuscate'

explanation.surface: A pair of performers begin muddying the story.
explanation.walkthrough: The join falls inside a word rather than between the two: the duet's own final T ends up opening the second word of the answer, which is why the enumeration reads 3,2.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Due to' and 'because of' are both prepositional phrases naming a cause, and either can replace the other in front of a noun.

clue.text: Following fart, Earth tremors

indicators.note: A tremor shakes things out of the places they were sitting in, and the letters beside it are what gets shaken.

parts.note: four letters of raw material, taken as printed
E = Earth, the astronomer's abbreviation for the planet

explanation.surface: A lavatorial cause and a seismic effect, in that order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earth tremors' is one phrase in the surface and two separate jobs underneath — the planet donates a letter and the shaking is the instruction, which is the split the schoolboy joke is there to hide.
explanation.definitionFit: After and following both mean coming later than something, and both work as prepositions: after the meeting, following the meeting.

clue.text: Rate increase for stall

parts.note: the rate a piece of music goes at is its tempo
an increase is a rise, as in a pay rise

explanation.surface: A rate increase of the sort that stops something in its tracks.
explanation.walkthrough: Both wordplay pieces are nouns and the answer is a verb, so the one-word definition has to carry all the grammar: 'stall' is what tells you the clue has changed part of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: To temporise is to spin things out to gain time, which is exactly what somebody stalling does — the two verbs swap directly.

clue.text: Man stopping agitated suspect leaving court in ancient city

indicators.note: Something stopping in a place has come to rest inside it, so the man's two letters halt in the middle of the rest.
The departure sense: what it names walks out of the fodder before anything is shuffled.
An agitated suspect will not sit still, and the letters standing next to the word do not stay in their given order either.

parts.note: SUSPECT drops CT, the abbreviation for court
a man is 'he' — the pronoun, not an abbreviation

explanation.surface: A man blocks an agitated suspect's path as they walk out of court.
explanation.walkthrough: Order matters: the court leaves first, and only what remains is stirred. Ephesus stood on the coast of what is now Turkey, and its temple of Artemis was one of the seven wonders.
explanation.definitionFit: Ephesus was a great Greek and later Roman city on the Aegean coast, ruined for centuries, so 'ancient city' names it by category.

clue.text: Where to find classic content to keep, somehow

indicators.note: 'content' is the noun — the stuff held inside a thing — so what is wanted sits within the words that follow rather than being described by them.

parts.note: five letters in an unbroken run across this span, the comma counting for nothing

explanation.surface: A tip about where to track down classic material worth hanging on to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classic content' reads as old films or records worth archiving, and a Classic is a horse race — one of five, two of them run on the Surrey downs every summer.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom Downs is the Surrey racecourse that stages the Derby and the Oaks, two of British flat racing's five Classics, so it is literally where a Classic is found.

clue.text: Some welcoming chief's utter lawlessness

indicators.note: To welcome somebody is to take them into your house, so one word opens up and lets the other sit inside it.

parts.note: 'some' and 'any' swap over in questions — have you some tea, have you any tea
arch- means the principal one: archbishop, arch-enemy

explanation.surface: A hospitable chief greets a few visitors, and total disorder follows.
explanation.walkthrough: ARCH for chief is the piece worth owning — the prefix in archbishop and arch-rival means the top one — and the apostrophe-s reads as a possessive when it is really standing in for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anarchy is the absence of government altogether, so 'utter' is fair: not disorder within the law but no law at all.

clue.text: Quickly leaving a relationship to keep some credibility, primarily

indicators.note: 'primarily' means first of all, so only the opening letters of the two words after it are wanted.

parts.note: used literally

indicators.note: To keep a thing is to hold on to it, so this word closes around what comes next and holds it in.

parts.note: bonding is what a relationship consists of — forming an attachment
the first letters of those two words

explanation.surface: Somebody walks out of a relationship fast, trying to keep a shred of credibility intact.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition stops after two words even though 'leaving a relationship' reads as a single idea, and that overrun is the trap: the relationship is raw material, not meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Absconding is going off in a hurry and without permission, so 'quickly leaving' matches it as an -ing phrase, with the sneaking away left implied.

clue.text: Crimean War conference site boosted at city close to Turkey

indicators.note: To boost a thing is to shove it upwards, and upwards in a down entry means the letters are read back towards the top of the grid.

parts.note: used literally
LA = Los Angeles, the city setters reach for first

indicators.note: 'close' is the ending sense, as in the close of play, so it takes the final letter of the word after it.

parts.note: the last letter of 'Turkey'

explanation.surface: A wartime summit venue being talked up in a city near the Turkish border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crimean War' invites the 1850s and the Charge of the Light Brigade; the conference meant here is the 1945 one, held in Crimea in the middle of an altogether different war.
explanation.definitionFit: Yalta, on the Crimean coast, hosted the February 1945 summit of Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin — a conference held in Crimea during a war.

clue.text: Small untruth by rector is more cunning

indicators.note: 'by' means beside here, as in standing by the door, so what it names is set down next to what has been built already.

parts.note: S = small, as on a clothes label
an untruth is a lie
R = rector, standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A little fib told in the rector's hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: The spelling is the whole difficulty: sly gives both slyer and slier, and only one of them can be built from the three pieces the clue hands over.
explanation.definitionFit: Slier is the comparative of sly, so it means more cunning — matching the definition in degree as well as in sense.

clue.text: Musical show Oscar's promoted in one advance article

indicators.note: Oscar is O in the phonetic alphabet, and promoting a letter in a down entry lifts it one place up the grid, past whatever sat above it.

parts.note: one = I, the Roman numeral
an advance of money is a loan
'the' is the definite article of English grammar

explanation.surface: Oscar has gone up in the world since the advance notice for the show came out.
explanation.walkthrough: Only one letter moves, and 'Oscar' names it rather than referring to a person or a statuette. Gilbert and Sullivan wrote the piece in 1882, poking fun at the peerage.
explanation.definitionFit: Iolanthe is Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera about a fairy and the House of Lords, staged constantly by amateur societies, so 'musical show' names its kind.

clue.text: Individual taking ecstasy

parts.note: somebody who is on a drug is taking it, which is how the slang runs
E = ecstasy, the standard abbreviation for the drug

explanation.surface: Somebody at a club has dropped a pill.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words of clue, two pieces of wordplay and a definition — the sort of miniature where the drug slang and the letters happen to say the same thing.
explanation.definitionFit: One is the pronoun for a single individual — 'the one on the left' — so the noun substitutes for it directly.

clue.text: I reprove criminal on the way out

indicators.note: A criminal is somebody who will not keep to the rules, and the letters beside the word will not keep to their order.

parts.note: eight letters of raw material, the setter's 'I' counted in

explanation.surface: The setter tells off a crook who is already halfway to the door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the way out' looks like a man leaving and means past its best — fruit rather than people. 'I' is the setter, and here it is fodder rather than a pronoun to read past.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit that is overripe is past its best and about to spoil, which is what 'on the way out' says as an idiom for something in decline.

clue.text: Husband visiting market in Hull

indicators.note: A visitor goes inside the place they are visiting, so the letter named lands in the middle of the other word.

parts.note: to market something is to sell it
H = husband, standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A husband doing the rounds of a market in a Yorkshire port.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull is a city on the Humber, which is what the capital letter and the whole sentence want you to think — and the definition is the ordinary noun, the casing round a nut.
explanation.definitionFit: A hull is the outer casing — of a boat, or of a seed or a nut — and a shell is that same hard covering round the contents.

clue.text: Most ale breaks down sugar

indicators.note: Whatever breaks down comes apart into its separate pieces, and pieces can be put back together in another order.

parts.note: seven letters of raw material, the two words run together

explanation.surface: Beer being digested, or a brew going bad in the barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: The chemistry in the surface is true, which is what makes it so easy to read straight past: malt sugar is precisely what ale is brewed out of, so fodder and answer describe one drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Maltose is malt sugar, the one starch turns into when grain is mashed, so 'sugar' names the chemical family it belongs to.

clue.text: Sickness resulting from excrement, mostly, around hovel

indicators.note: 'mostly' asks for most of the word and not all of it, so the final letter is left behind.
Something placed around a thing closes on both sides of it, so these letters end up either side of the hovel's.

parts.note: CRAP without its last letter
a hole is a hovel — the word you use of somewhere miserable to live

explanation.surface: An illness picked up from filthy sanitation in a slum dwelling.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is medically accurate — the disease really does travel in contaminated waste — and a clue that tells the truth is the hardest kind to notice you are being given wordplay in.
explanation.definitionFit: Cholera is an acute infection of the gut spread by dirty water, so 'sickness' is the general word standing in for the specific disease.

clue.text: Emperor announced what guards should do to escaping woman?

indicators.note: Something announced is said out loud, so what follows describes a sound and not a spelling.

parts.words: what guards should do to escaping woman?
parts.note: guards watching a woman make a run for it would grab her — say that order aloud and write down what you hear

explanation.surface: Guards being told what to do about a woman making a break for it.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the join between the two halves of the sound, which arrive as two words and land as one name.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar became the title every Roman emperor took after Julius, and the root of both Kaiser and Tsar, so 'Emperor' defines it by rank.

clue.text: Draw Forth Bridge's terminus, OK?

indicators.note: A terminus is the end of the line, so it asks for the last letter of what comes before it.

parts.note: the final letter of the name — the Forth Bridge is the great red railway crossing near Edinburgh
licit means permitted, lawful — the word illicit is built on it

explanation.surface: Somebody asks whether it is all right to sketch the far end of the Forth Bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw forth' is the phrase the surface offers and it is a word too long: Forth belongs to the bridge, which hands over a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To elicit an answer is to draw it out of somebody, so 'draw' is the verb in its extracting sense rather than its sketching one.

clue.text: Perhaps rib cracked by a silly prat in royal family

indicators.note: Silly behaviour is not orderly behaviour, so the letters next to the word come out in no sensible arrangement.
A cracked bone splits open, and what splits open here leaves a gap for the other letters to sit in.

parts.note: a rib is one bone among many, which is what 'perhaps' is flagging
those five letters put into another order

explanation.surface: Someone's rib gets broken by an idiot who has got in among the royals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royal family' sends you to the Windsors and the answer is French: Napoleon's people, emperors rather than kings, which is the geography the clue quietly relies on.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bonapartes were the French imperial dynasty Napoleon founded, so the surname names a royal family — by example, since it is one house among several.

clue.text: Jeer King James, perhaps

parts.note: to jeer at a performer is to boo
K = king, as on a chessboard or a playing card

explanation.surface: A crowd jeering King James.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King James' is one phrase on the surface and two separate jobs underneath, and the King James Bible sitting behind the name is the setter's joke rather than the parsing.
explanation.definitionFit: James is one of the letters of the New Testament, so it defines by example — a particular book standing in for the category.

clue.text: Pressure on animal sanctuary to provide recreation area

indicators.note: In a down entry 'on' stacks one piece on top of another, so the letter named sits above what follows.

parts.note: P = pressure, the physicist's abbreviation
Noah's ark took two of every animal aboard and kept them safe from the flood

explanation.surface: Campaigners lean on an animal shelter to open a recreation ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pressure on' reads as one phrase and it is two: the noun gives a letter, and the little word that follows tells you where to put it.
explanation.definitionFit: A park is public ground kept open for leisure, so 'recreation area' describes what one is for rather than offering a synonym.

clue.text: Working at home is boring Harry

indicators.note: To bore is to drill a hole into something, so the word sends what stands beside it into the middle.

parts.note: to harry somebody is to dog them, following and pestering
somebody at home is in

explanation.surface: Working from home is dull for Harry.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry is a verb wearing a capital letter, as setters like it to — to harry is to hound — and 'boring' is an instruction rather than a complaint about the job.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing and working match as gerunds: what are you doing and what are you working at name the same activity.

clue.text: Present introduction from Guardian and two shelfmates

indicators.note: An introduction is what comes at the front, so this takes the opening letter of the name after it.

parts.note: the first letter of the paper's name
the i is a British national daily, filed on the same newsagent's shelf
the FT is the Financial Times, the pink business daily — the second neighbour on that shelf

explanation.surface: A present, announced by this paper along with the two sold beside it.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is pointing at a newsagent's rack: the i and the FT are the two national dailies filed next to the paper the puzzle appears in, and naming its own masthead is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A gift is a present in the plainest sense: the thing handed over freely, with nothing to choose between the two words.

clue.text: Different native losing millions

indicators.note: Something losing a part no longer has it, so the letter named next drops out of the word before it.

parts.note: a mother tongue is a native tongue, and a mother country a native one
M = millions, and this is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A local man is losing millions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Native' as an adjective is the step to see — mother tongue, mother country — and once that word is on the page a single letter leaves it.
explanation.definitionFit: Other means not this one, which is what different means when two things are being contrasted: the other way round, a different way round.

clue.text: Claimant's straightforward argument

parts.note: plain speaking is straightforward speaking
a tiff is a small argument, the domestic kind

explanation.surface: A claimant putting a simple case to the court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Argument' means a case in the legal surface and a squabble in the wordplay, and the apostrophe-s that looks possessive is standing in for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The plaintiff is the party bringing a civil action, the one making the claim, so 'claimant' is the plainer English word for the same role.
